posts.name: Dan Niles
posts.text:
Thoughts around AI

1) Given AI is the largest technology revolution in history at roughly 3.5% of GPD (larger than electrification, highways & internet combined); there is overinvestment due to the potential rewards for the eventual winners.

2) But much like during the Internet buildout, which had several large drawdowns including in 1997 (Asian currency crisis) and 1998 (Russian bond default), and then ripped higher, the question is whether this is THE TOP.

3) AI had 3 separate investment waves: training, inference and now Agentic
a. Agentic demands 10-100x more tokens than inference and started with OpenClaw in January for the tech savvy followed by Muse in late September for the rest of us.

4) Currently, the market is repricing two things
a. Financing costs are higher in both debt & equity mkts
i. Debt- $CRWV unsecured debt trading at 15%

ii. Equity- expected timing for AI related IPOs like OpenAI, Anthropic delayed earlier this year while filed IPOs of Firmus, AirTrunk, NScale, SB Energy delayed/ pulled

iii. Meta 8K “timing is important to secure capital before competitors saturate various funding options… in an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital.”

b. AI native growth rates slowing
i. Anthropic revs 145% q/q in Q2 to 45% in Q3

ii. Openweight driving ASPs down ~50% since May

5) Datacenter moratoriums seem to be the only thing both parties agree on
a. This could get worse after the mid-terms with a less AI-friendly political climate

In summary, because of the advent of Agentic, I do not believe this is THE TOP. But having higher cash levels and being circumspect as the market reprices has been important. This has been my advice for the past several weeks.

Unfortunately, my belief that it was time to start putting money to work for at least a short-term rally this past week due to oversold conditions in areas like semiconductors has been early so far. The SOX was down 3.2% last week vs the S&P down 0.5% but time will tell.

$MSFT $AMZN $GOOGL earnings this upcoming wk
1) I think much like with $Meta earnings this past week where I previewed concerns, the stock reactions for the above three will have a lot more to do with their comments around future capex investments, expenses, cash flow and financing needs.

2) I worry whether a datacenter moratorium causes an issue with cloud growth guidance for the December quarter despite very strong growth in the September quarter. NextDC in Australia cut their rev guide by 22% for CY27 due to local community pushback and the stock was hit for 39% last week.

Microsoft seems committed to being cash flow positive and I see them being an ultimate winner in enterprise AI. 1. They provide a safe environment to run Co-Pilot AI applications given almost all S&P companies run M365 already. Co-Pilot seats were 30M+ in the June quarter up from 20M+ in March and 15M in December. 

2. One potential risk is their high margin PC business being impacted by the large declines being caused by surging memory prices. 

3. Azure expectations vs their guidance of 45% y/y for September vs 43% in June have also picked up given the share gains being seen by OpenAI against Anthropic recently in enterprise.

Google should see accelerating cloud growth & be an ultimate winner in consumer AI through their Android distribution on smartphones. My short-term concerns are the following:
1. Cash flow was negative for the first time since being a public company in the June quarter.

2. A slight miss in search revs in the June quarter raise concerns around AI Agents not looking at ads.

3. More aggressive analysts expect GCP growth of ~100% y/y for CQ3 y/y (but this includes TPU sales) up from 82% in CQ2 and 63% in Q1. This is more than double the growth rate expected for AWS and Azure so I worry that these datacenter moratoriums may on the margin impact the revenue growth possible at GCP.

posts.name: Jim O'Shaughnessy
posts.text:
That tracks with my experience. I've written 4 non-fiction books with my wife (who graduated summa cum laude with a degree in journalism) acting as primary editor.

The first thing she ever edited for me was a piece that Barron's published in 1992. I—having been the Editor-in-Chief of my High School newspaper and a long-time writer—thought the version I gave to her only needed a bit of polishing. 

What came back from her was a SEA of red ink with innumerable corrections and rewrites. 

I was livid! Not only was my ego crushed, I turned it into a huge fight with her, accusing her of trying to drain all of my wonderfully creative darlings out of the piece and replacing them with pedestrian prose for the sake of clarity. The fight got so heated we ended up not speaking about it for the rest of the day.

But then I dutifully went through my original draft and made all of the changes she recommended and the scales fell from eyes—her edited version of my original draft was VASTLY better than my draft. I immediately confessed this to her while simultaneously begging her to be the primary editor on the first book I wrote called "Invest Like the Best."

In hindsight, this was the best thing that could have ever happened to my writing career. Yes, I was emotionally wounded by the harsh criticism, but it was clearly needed. I'm of the opinion that ALL writers, no matter how gifted, could see their work materially improved by a gifted, honest to the point of inflicting emotional damage on the author editor. 

And here's the thing that made me create that vicious AI editor: At least for me, I don't get emotional when it's an AI editor dicing me up; had my wife or any other human editor been as brutal as the AI Editor, I undoubtedly would have been emotionally hurt and defensive. But since it was a machine, I was able to be far more dispassionate in my analysis of its feedback. I think it made my draft materially stronger. 

But now it's in the hands of my human editors at @infinitebooks so I must gird my emotions because while I can take it dispassionately from an AI editor, I no doubt will again take it emotionally when the humans tell me how much my work sucks. 

We humans are a strange and delightful species. 

https://x.com/jposhaughnessy/status/1277657154187603968

posts.text:
The US junk bond market is under severe pressure:

The effective yield on US CCC-rated and lower-rated high-yield corporate bonds is up to 18.0%, its highest level since the 2020 pandemic.

This figure has surged +500 basis points over the last 6 months, marking its largest 6-month increase since the 2022 bear market.

For perspective, this yield peaked at 45.0% during the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Meanwhile, credit spreads for CCC-rated and lower corporate bonds over Treasuries are up to 13.4%, the widest gap since July 2020.

Over the last 6 months, this gauge has risen +464 basis points, surpassing the 2022 bear market peak of 12.8%.

Cracks are widening beneath the surface of the credit market.

BREAKING: Japanese investors sold -$1.0 billion in foreign long-term bonds in the week ending October 17th, marking their 5th consecutive weekly sale, the longest such streak in 4 years.

Over this period, Japanese investors have sold a cumulative -$22.0 billion in foreign long-term debt securities.

Furthermore, the group sold -$1.0 billion in overseas short-term bonds in the week ending October 17th, marking their 2nd weekly sale over the last 3.

Year-to-date, sales of foreign debt by Japanese investors are up to -$33.0 billion, the largest outflow over the comparable period since 2022.

This also brought 12-month cumulative sales of foreign debt up to -$40.8 billion, the largest such outflow since April 2023.

This trend has been particularly driven by Japanese banks, which are increasing their domestic bond purchases amid historically attractive domestic bond yields.

The global bond market is experiencing a historic shift in investor demand.
